summary.text: For the cases corresponding to exponents \(2,3,4\), the congruence \(10^i\equiv1+9i\pmod M\) for \(M\mid81\), applied to a number and its reversal, forces \(M\) to divide its digit sum; this gives the all-nines number as a lower bound, while a cubing induction shows that this palindrome is divisible by the required power of \(3\).  For every larger exponent, repeat the palindromic block \(29799999792\) exactly \(3^{n-5}\) times: a finite divisibility check handles the initial block, each tripling of repetitions contributes another factor of \(3\), and its \(11\cdot3^{n-5}<3^{n-2}\) digits make it strictly smaller than the all-nines candidate.

full_proof.text:
Let \(\operatorname{rev}(m)\) denote the integer obtained by reversing the decimal digits of \(m\), with any zeros that become initial zeros discarded. For a positive integer \(N\), let \(a(N)\) be the least positive multiple \(x\) of \(N\) such that \(N\mid \operatorname{rev}(x)\), if such an \(x\) exists.

We prove that, for every \(n\ge 2\),
\[
a(3^n)=10^{3^{n-2}}-1
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
n\in\{2,3,4\}.
\]

We first establish that the number on the right-hand side of the proposed equality is always an admissible candidate.

### 1. The all-nines number is always an admissible candidate

We claim that for every \(k\ge 0\),
\[
3^{k+2}\mid 10^{3^k}-1. \tag{1}
\]
This follows by induction on \(k\). For \(k=0\), the assertion is simply
\[
3^2=9\mid 10-1=9.
\]
Suppose that \(3^{k+2}\mid A-1\), where
\[
A=10^{3^k}.
\]
Since \(10\equiv 1\pmod 3\), we have \(A\equiv 1\pmod 3\). Therefore
\[
A^2+A+1\equiv 1+1+1\equiv 0\pmod 3.
\]
Using
\[
A^3-1=(A-1)(A^2+A+1),
\]
the induction hypothesis supplies a factor \(3^{k+2}\) from the first factor and the displayed congruence supplies one further factor of \(3\) from the second. Hence
\[
3^{k+3}\mid A^3-1.
\]
But
\[
A^3=10^{3\cdot 3^k}=10^{3^{k+1}},
\]
so this is exactly the induction statement for \(k+1\). Thus (1) holds for all \(k\).

Now fix \(n\ge 2\), put
\[
D=3^{n-2},\qquad R=10^D-1.
\]
Taking \(k=n-2\) in (1) gives
\[
3^n\mid R. \tag{2}
\]
The decimal expansion of \(R\) consists of exactly \(D\) copies of the digit 9. It is consequently a palindrome, so
\[
\operatorname{rev}(R)=R.
\]
Thus (2) also gives \(3^n\mid\operatorname{rev}(R)\). Since \(R>0\), it is an admissible number in the definition of \(a(3^n)\). In particular, an admissible number always exists for these arguments, and
\[
a(3^n)\le R=10^{3^{n-2}}-1. \tag{3}
\]

We next develop a lower bound that will prove equality when \(n=2,3,4\).

### 2. A digit-sum divisibility lemma

Let \(m>0\) have decimal digits
\[
d_0,d_1,\ldots,d_{L-1},
\]
listed from least significant to most significant. Thus
\[
m=\sum_{i=0}^{L-1}d_i10^i,
\]
where \(0\le d_i\le 9\) and \(d_{L-1}\ne0\). Define
\[
S=\sum_{i=0}^{L-1}d_i,
\qquad
T=\sum_{i=0}^{L-1}i d_i.
\]
For the reversed digit list, define its weighted sum
\[
T'=\sum_{i=0}^{L-1}i d_{L-1-i}.
\]
A direct change of index gives
\[
T'=\sum_{i=0}^{L-1}(L-1-i)d_i,
\]
and hence
\[
T+T'=(L-1)S. \tag{4}
\]

Let \(M\) be any positive divisor of \(81\). Since \(10=1+9\), the binomial theorem gives, for every \(i\ge0\),
\[
10^i=(1+9)^i\equiv 1+9i\pmod {81},
\]
because every term after the linear term contains a factor \(9^2=81\). The same congruence therefore holds modulo \(M\). It follows that
\[
m=\sum_i d_i10^i\equiv S+9T\pmod M. \tag{5}
\]
Applying the same calculation to the reversed digit list gives
\[
\operatorname{rev}(m)\equiv S+9T'\pmod M. \tag{6}
\]
This remains valid even if the reversal begins with zeros, since those zeros do not alter the numerical value.

Suppose now that
\[
M\mid m\quad\text{and}\quad M\mid\operatorname{rev}(m).
\]
Equations (5) and (6) then yield
\[
S+9T\equiv0\pmod M,
\qquad
S+9T'\equiv0\pmod M.
\]
Adding and using (4), we obtain
\[
2S+9(T+T')
 =2S+9(L-1)S
 =(9L-7)S
 \equiv0\pmod M. \tag{7}
\]
Now
\[
9L-7\equiv -7\equiv2\pmod3,
\]
so \(3\nmid 9L-7\). Every prime divisor of \(M\), on the other hand, is \(3\), because \(M\mid81=3^4\). Hence
\[
\gcd(M,9L-7)=1.
\]
Cancelling the factor \(9L-7\) in (7), we conclude that
\[
M\mid S. \tag{8}
\]
Thus we have proved:

> If \(M\mid81\), and both a positive integer \(m\) and its decimal reversal are divisible by \(M\), then the decimal digit sum of \(m\) is divisible by \(M\).

We also need the following elementary consequence of a large digit sum.

> If a positive integer \(m\) has digit sum at least \(9D\), then
> \[
> m\ge 10^D-1. \tag{9}
> \]

Indeed, if \(m\) has \(L\) digits, its digit sum is at most \(9L\). Thus a digit sum of at least \(9D\) forces \(L\ge D\). If \(L>D\), then \(m\ge10^{L-1}\ge10^D>10^D-1\). If \(L=D\), then the digit sum is at most \(9D\), so it must equal \(9D\). Since each of the \(D\) digits is at most 9, equality is possible only if every digit is 9. In that case \(m=10^D-1\). This proves (9).

### 3. Equality for \(n=2,3,4\)

Let \(n\in\{2,3,4\}\), and put
\[
M=3^n,
\qquad
D=3^{n-2}.
\]
Then \(M\) is respectively \(9,27\), or \(81\), and in all three cases \(M\mid81\).

Let
\[
m=a(3^n).
\]
The all-nines witness from Section 1 shows that an admissible positive number exists. Therefore \(m>0\), and by the defining property of \(a\),
\[
3^n\mid m,
\qquad
3^n\mid\operatorname{rev}(m).
\]
Applying (8) with \(M=3^n\), we find that \(3^n\) divides the digit sum \(S\) of \(m\). Since \(m>0\), its digit sum is positive. Hence
\[
S\ge3^n.
\]
But
\[
3^n=3^2\cdot3^{n-2}=9D,
\]
so \(S\ge9D\). The lower bound (9) now gives
\[
m\ge10^D-1. \tag{10}
\]
On the other hand, (3) gives
\[
m\le10^D-1. \tag{11}
\]
Combining (10) and (11),
\[
a(3^n)=10^D-1=10^{3^{n-2}}-1.
\]
This proves equality for all three exponents. Concretely, the resulting values are
\[
a(9)=9,
\qquad
a(27)=999,
\qquad
a(81)=999999999.
\]

### 4. A smaller palindromic witness for every \(n\ge5\)

It remains to show that equality fails for all larger exponents. Consider the 11-digit palindrome
\[
B=29799999792.
\]
A direct division gives
\[
B=243\cdot122633744=3^5\cdot122633744. \tag{12}
\]

For each \(j\ge0\), define \(W_j\) to be the decimal integer obtained by concatenating \(3^j\) copies of the block \(29799999792\). Thus
\[
W_0=29799999792.
\]
Each block is a palindrome, and all the blocks are identical. Reversing the complete string reverses the order of the blocks and reverses each block; neither operation changes the resulting string. Therefore
\[
\operatorname{rev}(W_j)=W_j. \tag{13}
\]

We claim that
\[
3^{j+5}\mid W_j \qquad(j\ge0). \tag{14}
\]
For \(j=0\), this is exactly (12). Suppose (14) holds for some \(j\). The decimal length of \(W_j\) is
\[
L=11\cdot3^j.
\]
Since \(3^{j+1}=3\cdot3^j\), the number \(W_{j+1}\) consists of three consecutive copies of the complete decimal string for \(W_j\). Hence
\[
W_{j+1}
 =W_j10^{2L}+W_j10^L+W_j
 =W_j\bigl(1+10^L+10^{2L}\bigr). \tag{15}
\]
Modulo 3, \(10\equiv1\), and consequently
\[
1+10^L+10^{2L}\equiv1+1+1\equiv0\pmod3. \tag{16}
\]
The induction hypothesis says that \(W_j\) supplies a factor \(3^{j+5}\), while (16) says that the second factor in (15) supplies one further factor of 3. Thus
\[
3^{j+6}\mid W_{j+1},
\]
proving (14) by induction.

Now let \(n\ge5\) and take
\[
j=n-5.
\]
Then (14) gives
\[
3^n=3^{j+5}\mid W_j.
\]
Together with (13), this shows that both \(W_j\) and its reversal are divisible by \(3^n\). Hence \(W_j\) is an admissible candidate and
\[
a(3^n)\le W_j. \tag{17}
\]

It remains to compare its size with the all-nines candidate. The number \(W_j\) has exactly \(11\cdot3^j\) decimal digits, so
\[
W_j<10^{11\cdot3^j}. \tag{18}
\]
Since \(11<27\) and \(3^j>0\),
\[
11\cdot3^j<27\cdot3^j=3^{j+3}=3^{n-2}. \tag{19}
\]
For integer exponents, (19) implies
\[
10^{11\cdot3^j}\le 10^{3^{n-2}}-1. \tag{20}
\]
Indeed, the left side is a strictly smaller positive integral power of 10 than \(10^{3^{n-2}}\), and is therefore an integer strictly below it. Combining (18) and (20),
\[
W_j<10^{3^{n-2}}-1. \tag{21}
\]
Finally, (17) and (21) yield
\[
a(3^n)<10^{3^{n-2}}-1
\qquad(n\ge5). \tag{22}
\]
Thus the asserted equality is impossible for every \(n\ge5\).

For an arbitrary \(n\ge2\), either \(n\in\{2,3,4\}\), in which case Section 3 proves the equality, or \(n\ge5\), in which case Section 4 proves strict inequality. Therefore
\[
\boxed{
a(3^n)=10^{3^{n-2}}-1
\iff n=2\text{ or }n=3\text{ or }n=4
\quad(n\ge2).}
\]
